provenance: One-way snapshot derived from EI reference content (read-only). Owned and versioned by SelfAudit from this point on.

chg.adoption-design.title: Adoption Design
chg.adoption-design.plain_meaning:
Engineering the uptake of anything new — tool, process, policy —
through incentives that favor the new way, friction removed from
it and added to the old way, and communication that answers "what's
in it for me" honestly.

chg.change-management.title: Change Management
chg.change-management.plain_meaning:
Why initiatives fail at the humans, not the plan — and the craft of
moving people through change: urgency they believe, a coalition
that carries it, early wins that prove it, and persistence past the
point where leadership got bored.

chg.communication-cascades.title: Communication Cascades
chg.communication-cascades.plain_meaning:
Getting one message through many layers intact: the discipline of
equipping each level of management to carry the same story — because
every layer is a filter, and unmanaged filters compound into a
different message by the frontline.

chg.resistance-diagnosis.title: Resistance Diagnosis
chg.resistance-diagnosis.plain_meaning:
Sorting WHY people resist before treating it: can't (ability — they
lack skill, time, or tools), won't-because-it-costs-them (incentive
— the change genuinely harms their position), or won't-because-they-
don't-believe (conviction — they think it's wrong or doomed).
Different diseases, different cures.

chg.transformation-design.title: Transformation Design
chg.transformation-design.plain_meaning:
Sequencing big, multi-quarter change: the coalition before the
announcement, the beachhead before the rollout, quick wins placed
where skeptics watch, and a cadence that survives leadership's
attention span.

dat.bi-dashboards.title: BI & Dashboards
dat.bi-dashboards.plain_meaning:
Turning data into interfaces people actually check — Power BI, Tableau,
Looker — where the goal is decisions made faster, not charts made
prettier.

dat.data-modeling-warehousing.title: Data Modeling & Warehousing
dat.data-modeling-warehousing.plain_meaning:
Structuring data so questions are cheap: facts (events with numbers)
joined to conformed dimensions (customer, product, date meaning the
same thing everywhere) — Kimball's star schemas, or wider modern
variants, in a warehouse built for asking.

dat.data-quality.title: Data Quality
dat.data-quality.plain_meaning:
Whether the data is complete, current, consistent, and traceable to
its source — lineage, freshness, and the unglamorous audits that keep
"data-driven" from meaning "confidently misled."

dat.data-storytelling.title: Data Storytelling
dat.data-storytelling.plain_meaning:
Making numbers change minds: the finding stated as a headline, the
chart designed to show exactly that finding, and the so-what attached
— analysis packaged for a decision, not a data dump.

dat.etl-pipelines.title: ETL & Pipelines
dat.etl-pipelines.plain_meaning:
Moving and transforming data reliably from where it's created to where
it's questioned — extract, transform, load (or ELT, transforming after
landing) — the plumbing under every number anyone trusts.

dat.experimentation.title: Experimentation
dat.experimentation.plain_meaning:
A/B tests and their kin: deliberately varying one thing across
comparable groups so you learn what actually CAUSED what — the only
reliable escape from correlation's hall of mirrors.

dat.forecasting-methods.title: Forecasting Methods
dat.forecasting-methods.plain_meaning:
The statistical toolkit for predicting: baselines (naive, moving
average), decomposition (trend + seasonality + noise), exponential
smoothing and beyond — applications live in each pillar (demand,
financial, pipeline); the craft lives here.

dat.goodharts-law.title: Goodhart's Law
dat.goodharts-law.plain_meaning:
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure —
the moment a number decides pay, promotion, or survival, people
optimize the NUMBER, and its connection to the thing it measured
starts dissolving.

dat.metric-design.title: Metric Design
dat.metric-design.plain_meaning:
Choosing and structuring the numbers a company steers by: a metric
tree from north star down to team-level drivers, leading indicators
ahead of lagging ones, and paired metrics that watch each other's
blind sides.

dat.predictive-analytics.title: Predictive Analytics
dat.predictive-analytics.plain_meaning:
Models that score the future at the individual level: which customer
will churn, which lead will convert, which invoice will pay late —
pattern recognition dressed as foresight, useful exactly as far as
tomorrow resembles the training data.

dat.spreadsheets.title: Spreadsheets
dat.spreadsheets.plain_meaning:
Excel and Sheets as the universal modeling tool — the fastest way to
think in numbers ever built, and the least governed system in every
company that runs on it.

dat.sql.title: SQL
dat.sql.plain_meaning:
The language for asking databases questions directly — joins, filters,
aggregations — the difference between waiting in the analytics queue
and knowing in ninety seconds.

dat.statistics-fundamentals.title: Statistics Fundamentals
dat.statistics-fundamentals.plain_meaning:
Enough statistics to not fool yourself: distributions (averages hide
shapes), variance (this month's jump may be noise), significance (would
this difference survive a coin-flip test), and the eternal gap between
correlation and cause.

ent.exit-paths.title: Exit Paths
ent.exit-paths.plain_meaning:
How ownership ends: acquisition (strategic or financial), IPO,
secondaries (partial founder liquidity), management buyout, or a
well-run shutdown — each with different preparation, timelines, and
masters.

ent.founder-led-sales.title: Founder-Led Sales
ent.founder-led-sales.plain_meaning:
The founder personally selling the first customers — not because
sales hires are unaffordable, but because the founder is the only
one who can afford to hear the truth the market is telling.

ent.founder-psychology.title: Founder Psychology
ent.founder-psychology.plain_meaning:
The mental load of the job: decision fatigue, isolation, identity
fused to the company, and the specific distortions (grandiosity on
Monday, doom on Wednesday) that pressure produces in otherwise
sound judgment.

ent.fundraising-strategy.title: Fundraising Strategy
ent.fundraising-strategy.plain_meaning:
Whether to raise at all, when, how much, and from whom — the
strategic layer above the term-sheet mechanics (which live in
Finance). Money always arrives with a worldview attached.

ent.scaling-pathologies.title: Scaling Pathologies
ent.scaling-pathologies.plain_meaning:
The characteristic diseases of growing fast: premature scaling
(spending like the model works before it does), culture dilution
(hiring faster than values transmit), and process debt (systems
built for 10 people operating 60).

ent.stage-transitions.title: Stage Transitions
ent.stage-transitions.plain_meaning:
What breaks as the company grows through stages — 5 to 20 to 50 to
150 people — where each transition demands that yesterday's survival
skills be partially retired, on schedule, before their absence
becomes the crisis.

ent.zero-to-one.title: Zero to One
ent.zero-to-one.plain_meaning:
Idea to validated demand to first revenue: the search phase, where
the job is not building a company but discovering whether one should
exist — cheaply, fast, and against your own optimism.

ext.contracts.title: Contracts
ext.contracts.plain_meaning:
Promises with teeth: who does what, who pays what, what happens when
things go wrong — where the boring clauses (termination, liability,
renewal, IP) matter more than the business terms everyone actually
negotiates.

ext.corporate-governance.title: Corporate Governance
ext.corporate-governance.plain_meaning:
Who the company answers to and how: the board, fiduciary duties,
shareholder rights, and the machinery (minutes, approvals,
committees) that separates an accountable company from a founder
with a checkbook.

ext.esg-sustainability.title: ESG & Sustainability
ext.esg-sustainability.plain_meaning:
Environmental, social, and governance obligations treated as business
inputs: emissions and supply-chain footprints, labor practices, and
the reporting scaffolding that large customers, lenders, and
regulators increasingly demand of everyone they touch.

ext.geopolitics-policy.title: Geopolitics & Policy
ext.geopolitics-policy.plain_meaning:
How governments and geography move the markets you're in: trade
rules and tariffs, sanctions, industrial policy, data localization,
and the slow rewiring of supply chains along political lines.

ext.intellectual-property.title: Intellectual Property
ext.intellectual-property.plain_meaning:
Owning what you create: trademarks (your name and marks), copyright
(your code and content), patents (your inventions, maybe), and trade
secrets (what you deliberately keep confidential) — four different
tools with different costs and lifespans.

ext.legal-fundamentals.title: Legal Fundamentals
ext.legal-fundamentals.plain_meaning:
The operating minimum: entity structure (what shields what),
liability (who can be sued for which failures), and the judgment
call every operator faces weekly — what needs a lawyer versus what
needs a template versus what needs neither.

ext.macroeconomics.title: Macroeconomics
ext.macroeconomics.plain_meaning:
Cycles, interest rates, inflation, and currency as business inputs:
the weather system every company operates inside, ignorable in calm
years and decisive in the others.

ext.privacy-data-protection.title: Privacy & Data Protection
ext.privacy-data-protection.plain_meaning:
Handling personal data lawfully — GDPR, CCPA and their spreading
cousins: collect with a basis, use for the stated purpose, keep only
what's needed, delete on request, and tell the truth when breached.

ext.regulation-compliance.title: Regulation & Compliance
ext.regulation-compliance.plain_meaning:
The rules of your industry — licensing, reporting, sector-specific
law — and the operating posture toward them: compliant, compliant-ish,
or betting the company on nobody looking.

fin.accounting-fundamentals.title: Accounting Fundamentals
fin.accounting-fundamentals.plain_meaning:
The language of financial record: accrual vs cash basis, debits and credits,
when revenue counts as earned and when a cost counts as incurred — the rules
that decide what the numbers even mean.

fin.accounts-receivable.title: Accounts Receivable
fin.accounts-receivable.plain_meaning:
Money customers owe you for delivered work — revenue that exists on paper
but hasn't become cash yet.

fin.break-even.title: Break-even
fin.break-even.plain_meaning:
The volume (or revenue) at which the business stops losing money: fixed
costs divided by contribution margin per unit. Below it, every month costs
you; above it, every unit is profit.

fin.budgeting-fpa.title: Budgeting & FP&A
fin.budgeting-fpa.plain_meaning:
Planning what the business will spend and earn, then holding the plan
against reality every month — financial planning and analysis as the
company's steering feedback loop.

fin.capital-structure.title: Capital Structure
fin.capital-structure.plain_meaning:
The mix of debt and equity funding the business — cheap-but-demanding
money (debt: fixed obligations, covenants, someone who can force
outcomes) versus expensive-but-patient money (equity: dilution,
alignment, no repayment clock).

fin.cash-flow.title: Cash Flow
fin.cash-flow.plain_meaning:
Actual cash moving in and out over a period — operating, investing,
financing. Profit is an accounting opinion; cash is a fact.

fin.cash-runway.title: Cash Runway
fin.cash-runway.plain_meaning:
Cash in the bank divided by net monthly burn — how many months until zero.
The survival clock.

fin.cogs.title: COGS
fin.cogs.plain_meaning:
Cost of goods sold — what it directly costs to deliver the thing you sold.
Materials, direct labour, inbound and outbound freight, packaging.

fin.ebitda-net-margin.title: EBITDA & Net Margin
fin.ebitda-net-margin.plain_meaning:
Two depths of profitability: EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax,
depreciation, amortization) shows what the operating machine earns;
net margin shows what's actually left after everything, including the
things EBITDA politely ignores.

fin.financial-forecasting.title: Financial Forecasting
fin.financial-forecasting.plain_meaning:
Projecting the financial future — revenue, costs, cash — as honestly as the
evidence allows, with stated assumptions instead of embedded hopes.

fin.financial-statements.title: Financial Statements
fin.financial-statements.plain_meaning:
The three linked reports — P&L (performance over a period), balance sheet
(position at a moment), cash flow statement (where money actually moved) —
read together as one story, never separately.

fin.fundraising-mechanics.title: Fundraising Mechanics
fin.fundraising-mechanics.plain_meaning:
The fine print of other people's money: dilution math, SAFEs and
priced rounds, liquidation preferences, pro-rata rights, board seats,
vesting, and the cap table where every past decision lives forever.

fin.gross-margin.title: Gross Margin
fin.gross-margin.plain_meaning:
Money left after the direct cost of delivering what you sold.
Revenue minus COGS, usually shown as a percentage of revenue.

fin.operating-expenses.title: Operating Expenses
fin.operating-expenses.plain_meaning:
The cost of running the machine — salaries, rent, software, marketing,
admin — everything below gross margin that isn't directly tied to
delivering one unit.

fin.pricing-mathematics.title: Pricing Mathematics
fin.pricing-mathematics.plain_meaning:
The arithmetic of what a price change actually does — to margin, to
break-even volume, and to profit — before psychology or strategy enter
the room.

fin.revenue.title: Revenue
fin.revenue.plain_meaning:
Money earned from customers for goods or services delivered in a period.
Not the same as cash received, and not all revenue is equal quality.

fin.roi-irr-npv.title: ROI, IRR & NPV
fin.roi-irr-npv.plain_meaning:
Three ways to compare money spent now against money returned later:
ROI (simple return ratio), NPV (future cash discounted to today's value),
IRR (the discount rate at which a project breaks even). All three answer
one question — is this use of money better than the alternatives?

fin.unit-economics.title: Unit Economics
fin.unit-economics.plain_meaning:
Whether ONE unit of the business makes money: one customer, one order, one
seat, one job — its contribution margin after everything it directly causes,
including the cost of acquiring it.

fin.valuation.title: Valuation
fin.valuation.plain_meaning:
What a business is worth and the three ways to argue it: intrinsic
(discounted future cash flows), relative (multiples of comparable
companies), and transactional (what similar businesses actually sold
for) — three lenses that should triangulate, and interestingly argue
when they don't.

fin.working-capital.title: Working Capital
fin.working-capital.plain_meaning:
Cash trapped in the operating cycle — inventory sitting on shelves plus
money customers owe you, minus money you owe suppliers.

mi.competitive-intelligence.title: Competitive Intelligence
mi.competitive-intelligence.plain_meaning:
Watching rivals systematically — pricing moves, hiring patterns,
product releases, customer wins and losses — turned into a running
picture of their strategy and its next move.

mi.customer-interviews.title: Customer Interviews
mi.customer-interviews.plain_meaning:
Structured conversations that extract truth from customers — about
their past behavior, their actual workflow, what they've already
tried and spent — while defusing the politeness that makes people
lie encouragingly.

mi.market-research-methods.title: Market Research Methods
mi.market-research-methods.plain_meaning:
Primary research (talking to and observing the market yourself) and
secondary research (reports, data, other people's studies) — run to
produce truth you can act on, not comfort you can present.

mi.market-sizing.title: Market Sizing
mi.market-sizing.plain_meaning:
TAM, SAM, SOM done honestly: total market if everyone bought,
the slice your model can actually serve, the share you can win in
the planning horizon — built bottom-up from real units, not
top-down from a Gartner number.

mi.trend-analysis.title: Trend Analysis
mi.trend-analysis.plain_meaning:
Separating weak signals from noise before they're obvious: watching
the edges (early adopters, adjacent industries, cost curves,
regulation drafts) for what changes the game while it's still cheap
to act on.

mi.voice-of-customer.title: Voice of Customer
mi.voice-of-customer.plain_meaning:
The always-on listening system — surveys, NPS, reviews, support
themes, sales-call patterns — aggregated into signal about what
customers experience, want, and are starting to resent.

mi.win-loss-analysis.title: Win-Loss Analysis
mi.win-loss-analysis.plain_meaning:
Learning from every deal won and lost — from the BUYER's mouth, not
the rep's memory — why they chose what they chose, what almost
changed their mind, and who else was in the room.

mkt.brand-strategy.title: Brand Strategy
mkt.brand-strategy.plain_meaning:
Building memory structures in buyers' heads — being thought of at all when
the buying moment arrives, and being recognized instantly when seen — so
that future demand costs less to capture.

mkt.cac-ltv-attribution.title: CAC, LTV & Attribution
mkt.cac-ltv-attribution.plain_meaning:
What acquiring a customer fully costs (CAC), what a customer is worth over
their life (LTV), and which activity actually caused the acquisition
(attribution) — the three numbers that decide whether growth spending is
investment or bonfire.

mkt.customer-segmentation.title: Customer Segmentation
mkt.customer-segmentation.plain_meaning:
Splitting the market into groups that buy differently — different problems,
different budgets, different buying processes — so the business can choose
whom to serve instead of averaging everyone.

mkt.customer-success.title: Customer Success
mkt.customer-success.plain_meaning:
Making customers actually succeed with what they bought — onboarding to
first value fast, monitoring health, intervening before trouble — so
revenue stays and grows instead of quietly leaving.

mkt.demand-generation.title: Demand Generation
mkt.demand-generation.plain_meaning:
Creating qualified interest on purpose: the portfolio of paid, organic,
outbound, events, and referral activity that fills the top of the funnel
with people who resemble the ICP.

mkt.discounting.title: Discounting
mkt.discounting.plain_meaning:
Selling below list price to close volume. A price cut wearing a
deal-by-deal disguise.

mkt.expansion-nrr.title: Expansion & NRR
mkt.expansion-nrr.plain_meaning:
Growing revenue inside existing accounts — upsell, cross-sell, usage
growth — measured as net revenue retention: what last year's customers
pay this year, expansion minus churn, with no new logos counted.

mkt.funnel-conversion.title: Funnel & Conversion
mkt.funnel-conversion.plain_meaning:
The staged path from stranger to customer — visit, lead, qualified,
proposal, closed — measured as conversion rates between stages, so you
can see WHERE interest dies instead of just THAT it dies.

mkt.go-to-market.title: Go-To-Market
mkt.go-to-market.plain_meaning:
The motion that carries product to customer: self-serve/product-led,
inside sales, field sales, channel partners — and the choice of which,
for which segment, at which price point.

mkt.ideal-customer-profile.title: Ideal Customer Profile
mkt.ideal-customer-profile.plain_meaning:
The narrow, written definition of who you serve best and first: the
customer for whom your product is a painkiller, who can pay, who you can
reach, and who succeeds fast enough to stay and refer.

mkt.messaging.title: Messaging
mkt.messaging.plain_meaning:
Turning positioning into words that convert: the headlines, pitches, and
page copy that make the right buyer say "that's me, that's my problem,
I want that outcome."

mkt.organic-content-seo.title: Organic & Content
mkt.organic-content-seo.plain_meaning:
Earning attention that compounds instead of renting it: content, SEO,
community, and social presence that keep producing demand after the work
is paid for.

mkt.outbound-sales.title: Outbound Sales
mkt.outbound-sales.plain_meaning:
Cold outreach as a system: lists built from the ICP, sequenced touches
across email/phone/social, and qualification of whoever responds — demand
you go get instead of demand that finds you.

mkt.paid-acquisition.title: Paid Acquisition
mkt.paid-acquisition.plain_meaning:
Buying attention in auctions — search, social, display — and converting it
profitably. Rented demand: it arrives fast and stops the day you stop paying.

mkt.pipeline-forecasting.title: Pipeline Forecasting
mkt.pipeline-forecasting.plain_meaning:
Predicting bookings from the pipeline — stage-weighted, evidence-based,
and honest about the difference between commit, best case, and hope.

mkt.pipeline-management.title: Pipeline Management
mkt.pipeline-management.plain_meaning:
Keeping the deal inventory honest: right stages, real close dates, dead
deals removed — the pipeline as a truthful picture of future revenue
rather than a museum of optimism.

mkt.positioning.title: Positioning
mkt.positioning.plain_meaning:
The slot you occupy in the customer's mind relative to alternatives —
what category they file you under, whom they compare you against, and
what they expect you to cost before you say a word.

mkt.pricing-strategy.title: Pricing Strategy
mkt.pricing-strategy.plain_meaning:
What you charge, whom you charge it to, and what the price says about you —
the strategic layer above the arithmetic (which lives in Pricing
Mathematics). Value-based vs cost-plus vs competitor-matched; the metric
you charge on; the fences between tiers.

mkt.retention-churn.title: Retention & Churn
mkt.retention-churn.plain_meaning:
Whether customers stay and buy again. Churn is customers leaving —
quietly first, visibly later.

mkt.sales-compensation.title: Sales Compensation
mkt.sales-compensation.plain_meaning:
How sellers are paid — base, commission, bonuses — and critically,
what the variable part is calculated on.

mkt.sales-process.title: Sales Process
mkt.sales-process.plain_meaning:
The repeatable steps from lead to close — discovery, demo, proposal,
negotiation — each with entry and EXIT criteria, so a deal's stage means
the same thing regardless of whose deal it is.

mkt.sales-qualification.title: Sales Qualification
mkt.sales-qualification.plain_meaning:
Deciding fast which deals deserve time — testing for budget, authority,
need, timeline (BANT) or the deeper MEDDIC evidence — so selling effort
goes where it can actually convert.

mkt.value-proposition.title: Value Proposition
mkt.value-proposition.plain_meaning:
The promise of value that makes switching worth it: what the customer gets,
compared to what they'd otherwise do, minus the pain of change. Not a
slogan — an equation the buyer runs in their head.

ops.capacity-planning.title: Capacity Planning
ops.capacity-planning.plain_meaning:
Matching what you CAN deliver to what you'll be ASKED to deliver —
ahead of time, because capacity takes months to add and demand takes
one good quarter to outrun it.

ops.continuous-improvement.title: Continuous Improvement
ops.continuous-improvement.plain_meaning:
The habit of making the process better every cycle — small, constant,
owned by the people doing the work — rather than periodic improvement
projects done TO the work by outsiders.

ops.demand-planning.title: Demand Planning
ops.demand-planning.plain_meaning:
Forecasting what customers will order, so purchasing and capacity can
prepare ahead of time.

ops.inventory-management.title: Inventory Management
ops.inventory-management.plain_meaning:
The stock you hold to serve demand — raw materials, work in progress,
finished goods. Frozen cash sitting on shelves.

ops.lean-thinking.title: Lean Thinking
ops.lean-thinking.plain_meaning:
Removing waste from flow — everything the customer wouldn't pay for:
overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, inventory, motion,
defects — so value moves continuously instead of sitting in piles.

ops.logistics-warehousing.title: Logistics & Warehousing
ops.logistics-warehousing.plain_meaning:
Moving and storing goods without eating the margin: warehouse layout,
picking efficiency, carrier choice, and the last mile — the physical
plumbing between promise and doorstep.

ops.operational-kpis.title: Operational KPIs
ops.operational-kpis.plain_meaning:
The few numbers that actually steer the operation — chosen so that when
they move, someone knows what to do, and paired so that gaming one shows
up in another.

ops.operations-strategy.title: Operations Strategy
ops.operations-strategy.plain_meaning:
Choosing what your operation is BEST at — cost, speed, quality,
flexibility, or dependability — because physics lets you excel at one or
two, and pretending to excel at all five means excelling at none.

ops.order-fulfillment.title: Order Fulfillment
ops.order-fulfillment.plain_meaning:
The promise-to-delivery pipeline — receive the order, pick it, pack it,
ship it, deliver it right and on time.

ops.process-design.title: Process Design
ops.process-design.plain_meaning:
Building repeatable flows on purpose: each step with an owner, an input
standard, an output standard, and a reason to exist — instead of workflows
that congealed from history.

ops.procurement.title: Procurement
ops.procurement.plain_meaning:
Buying well: choosing vendors, negotiating terms, and managing the
relationship afterward — with total cost of ownership as the yardstick,
not the sticker price.

ops.quality-management.title: Quality Management
ops.quality-management.plain_meaning:
Preventing defects systematically — building quality into the process —
instead of inspecting them out at the end, after the cost is already sunk.

ops.service-delivery.title: Service Delivery
ops.service-delivery.plain_meaning:
Delivering intangible promises repeatedly — support, implementations,
managed services, agencies — where the product is an experience produced
live, every time, by people and process under load.

ops.sla-management.title: SLA Management
ops.sla-management.plain_meaning:
Explicit service promises — response times, uptime, delivery windows —
with defined measurement, honest reporting, and real consequences when
they're missed.

ops.sop-standard-work.title: SOPs & Standard Work
ops.sop-standard-work.plain_meaning:
The written best-known-way to do each recurring task — not bureaucracy,
but the current champion method, documented so quality survives turnover
and improvement has a baseline to beat.

ops.supply-chain.title: Supply Chain
ops.supply-chain.plain_meaning:
The network that turns orders into delivered goods — suppliers, factories,
warehouses, carriers — where your promise to customers is only as good as
the weakest, slowest, or most distant link you depend on.

ops.theory-of-constraints.title: Theory of Constraints
ops.theory-of-constraints.plain_meaning:
Every system has exactly one binding constraint at a time, and the whole
system moves at its pace — so improvement anywhere else is decoration,
and an hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost forever.

ops.workforce-scheduling.title: Workforce & Scheduling
ops.workforce-scheduling.plain_meaning:
Right people, right skills, right hours — matched against demand curves
that refuse to be flat: daily peaks, weekly rhythms, seasonal swells.

ppl.coaching-development.title: Coaching & Development
ppl.coaching-development.plain_meaning:
Growing people deliberately — through stretch assignments, real-time
coaching, and honest career conversations — instead of hoping experience
alone teaches.

ppl.compensation.title: Compensation
ppl.compensation.plain_meaning:
Paying competitively against the market while staying fair internally —
base, variable, and equity as one designed system rather than a pile of
negotiation outcomes.

ppl.conflict-resolution.title: Conflict Resolution
ppl.conflict-resolution.plain_meaning:
Turning friction into information: surfacing disagreement early, sorting
what it's actually about (facts, interests, or dignity), and closing it
with a decision people can commit to — instead of letting it ferment
into politics.

ppl.culture.title: Culture
ppl.culture.plain_meaning:
The behavior that gets rewarded, punished, and tolerated when nobody's
watching — the company's real operating system, as opposed to the values
on the wall.

ppl.executive-communication.title: Executive Communication
ppl.executive-communication.plain_meaning:
Saying hard things clearly to the people who need them — upward to boards
and investors, downward through layers, outward to customers and partners
— with the conclusion first and the evidence behind it.

ppl.hiring.title: Hiring
ppl.hiring.plain_meaning:
Sourcing, assessing, and closing people — the decision that compounds
more than any other, because every hire then hires, teaches, and sets
the bar for the next.

ppl.incentive-design.title: Incentive Design
ppl.incentive-design.plain_meaning:
Engineering what actually gets rewarded — pay, promotion, praise, and
what leadership visibly tolerates — knowing that people optimize for the
real reward system, not the stated one.

ppl.key-person-dependency.title: Key-Person Dependency
ppl.key-person-dependency.plain_meaning:
When one irreplaceable human is a single point of failure — the only one
who knows the system, holds the relationships, or makes the thing work —
and their bus factor is the company's.

ppl.leadership.title: Leadership
ppl.leadership.plain_meaning:
Getting sustained performance from people who could leave — through
direction they believe, standards they respect, and the daily evidence
that the leader absorbs pressure instead of amplifying it.

ppl.negotiation.title: Negotiation
ppl.negotiation.plain_meaning:
Claiming and creating value across a table — price, terms, roles, deals —
where preparation, alternatives, and listening beat aggression almost
every time.

ppl.organizational-design.title: Organizational Design
ppl.organizational-design.plain_meaning:
Who reports to whom, who decides what, and how wide each manager's span
runs — the structure through which strategy either flows or gets stuck.

ppl.performance-management.title: Performance Management
ppl.performance-management.plain_meaning:
Clear expectations, honest feedback against them, and real consequences
both ways — the loop that tells every person where they stand and the
company where its people are.

ppl.stakeholder-management.title: Stakeholder Management
ppl.stakeholder-management.plain_meaning:
Mapping who can help, block, or quietly sabotage what you're trying to do
— then deliberately managing their information, involvement, and interests
instead of hoping merit speaks for itself.

ppl.team-effectiveness.title: Team Effectiveness
ppl.team-effectiveness.plain_meaning:
Why some groups multiply their members and others divide them: trust,
productive conflict, real commitment, mutual accountability, and shared
results — Lencioni's stack, in that order, because each layer requires
the one below.

prd.customer-discovery.title: Customer Discovery
prd.customer-discovery.plain_meaning:
Learning what customers actually need — through interviews about their
past behavior, observation of their workflow, and small tests — without
leading the witness or pitching disguised as research.

prd.design-ux.title: Design & UX
prd.design-ux.plain_meaning:
Making the product usable enough that its value survives contact with
real users — reducing the distance between what someone wants to do and
what the interface lets them do without thinking.

prd.jobs-to-be-done.title: Jobs To Be Done
prd.jobs-to-be-done.plain_meaning:
What customers actually hire the product to accomplish — the progress
they're trying to make in a situation — rather than who they are
demographically or what features they click.

prd.platform-ecosystem.title: Platform & Ecosystem
prd.platform-ecosystem.plain_meaning:
When others build on you — integrations, apps, marketplaces, APIs — and
value comes from the network between participants, not just your own
features.

prd.product-analytics.title: Product Analytics
prd.product-analytics.plain_meaning:
The product's vital signs: activation (reached first value), engagement
(uses it, how deeply, how often), and retention cohorts (still here after
N weeks) — measured per cohort, not as vanity totals.

prd.product-development-process.title: Product Development Process
prd.product-development-process.plain_meaning:
How ideas become shipped product — the batch size, cycle length, and
decision rituals: scrum sprints, kanban flow, Shape Up cycles, or the
unnamed thing a team actually does regardless of what it calls itself.

prd.product-led-growth.title: Product-Led Growth
prd.product-led-growth.plain_meaning:
The product itself as the acquisition, conversion, and expansion channel:
try before buy, value before paywall, and usage that naturally spreads to
teammates — the motion where the product does the selling.

prd.product-market-fit.title: Product-Market Fit
prd.product-market-fit.plain_meaning:
The state where the market pulls the product out of you — customers stay,
use it more, and bring others — instead of every sale being pushed uphill.
Not a feeling; measurable in retention curves and pull signals.

prd.product-operations.title: Product Operations
prd.product-operations.plain_meaning:
The connective tissue that keeps product teams running on data instead of
folklore: instrumentation that works, research that's findable, launch
processes that repeat, and feedback loops that route to the right owner.

prd.product-strategy.title: Product Strategy
prd.product-strategy.plain_meaning:
Which problems the product will solve, for whom, in what order — and,
just as loudly, which it will refuse. The connective layer between company
strategy and what engineers build this quarter.

prd.roadmap-prioritization.title: Roadmap Prioritization
prd.roadmap-prioritization.plain_meaning:
Sequencing what gets built against impact, confidence, and effort — and
defending that sequence against the daily assault of new urgencies.

rea.calibration-learning.title: Calibration & Learning
rea.calibration-learning.plain_meaning:
Keeping score on your own judgment: writing predictions down before
outcomes arrive, reviewing the misses without flinching, and updating how
confident you're allowed to be next time.

rea.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis
rea.diagnosis.plain_meaning:
Finding the verified first cause of a problem — the domino that fell first —
rather than the symptom that finally became visible or the explanation that
arrived first.

rea.judgment-under-uncertainty.title: Judgment Under Uncertainty
rea.judgment-under-uncertainty.plain_meaning:
Deciding as if placing a bet: probabilities instead of certainties, payoffs
weighed against odds, and the quality of the decision judged separately from
the luck of the outcome.

rea.prioritization.title: Prioritization
rea.prioritization.plain_meaning:
Ranking what gets done first by impact and leverage — and keeping an
explicit not-now list, because a priority list without a sacrifice list
is just a wish list.

rea.second-order-thinking.title: Second-order Thinking
rea.second-order-thinking.plain_meaning:
Tracing consequences past the first step: "and then what?" — including the
step where other people (customers, competitors, employees) adapt to what
you just did.

rea.structuring.title: Structuring
rea.structuring.plain_meaning:
Turning a messy situation into a defined problem before trying to solve it —
a one-sentence problem statement, then a tree of possible causes or options
that is MECE: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive.

rea.systems-thinking.title: Systems Thinking
rea.systems-thinking.plain_meaning:
Seeing a business as loops, stocks, and delays instead of isolated events —
where today's problem is usually yesterday's solution feeding back, and the
structure of the system produces its behavior more than the people in it do.

rea.trade-off-analysis.title: Trade-off Analysis
rea.trade-off-analysis.plain_meaning:
Naming what every option sacrifices — because in a functioning market and a
finite company, every real choice buys something by giving something up.
An option with no visible downside just has an unexamined one.

rsk.business-continuity.title: Business Continuity
rsk.business-continuity.plain_meaning:
Surviving the bad day: backups that restore, failovers that fail
over, plans that name who does what when systems, buildings, vendors,
or people are suddenly unavailable — tested before needed, because
the test IS the plan.

rsk.concentration-risk.title: Concentration Risk
rsk.concentration-risk.plain_meaning:
Too much of anything vital in one place: one customer as 40% of
revenue, one supplier for the critical input, one channel for all
demand, one person holding the system, one geography holding the
infrastructure.

rsk.cyber-risk.title: Cyber Risk
rsk.cyber-risk.plain_meaning:
Security posture translated into business risk: what an attack
would actually cost (downtime, data, ransom, trust, lawyers), how
likely your current hygiene makes it, and which defenses buy the
most risk reduction per dollar.

rsk.data-governance.title: Data Governance
rsk.data-governance.plain_meaning:
Policy for who owns, accesses, and answers for data: ownership per
domain, access rules, retention schedules, definition authority —
the accountability layer that data quality, privacy, and security
all stand on.

rsk.internal-controls.title: Internal Controls
rsk.internal-controls.plain_meaning:
Process checks that make error and fraud hard: separation of duties
(no one both approves and pays), reconciliations (two records that
must agree), approval thresholds, and access limits — friction
installed on purpose where money and data move.

rsk.risk-appetite.title: Risk Appetite
rsk.risk-appetite.plain_meaning:
Deciding in advance how much risk is acceptable, per domain: where
the company bets boldly (product, growth experiments), where it's
conservative (cash, compliance, security), and how big any single
bet may be — written before the exciting opportunity arrives.

rsk.risk-process.title: Risk Process
rsk.risk-process.plain_meaning:
The loop: identify → assess (likelihood × impact) → treat (avoid,
reduce, transfer, accept) → monitor — run as a standing rhythm, not
a binder produced once for an audit.

rsk.risk-taxonomy.title: Risk Taxonomy
rsk.risk-taxonomy.plain_meaning:
Naming the kinds of risk so none hide: strategic (wrong bets),
operational (broken processes), financial (cash, credit, market),
compliance (rules), cyber, reputational, and concentration — a
shared vocabulary that turns "what keeps you up at night" into a
checklist.

rsk.vendor-risk.title: Vendor Risk
rsk.vendor-risk.plain_meaning:
Third parties as extensions of your risk surface: every critical
vendor's outage is your outage, their breach is your breach, their
price increase is your margin call — inherited exposure you chose
by signing.

str.business-model-design.title: Business Model Design
str.business-model-design.plain_meaning:
How the company creates, delivers, and captures value — who pays, for
what, how often, at what margin, through what cost structure. The
architecture of the money.

str.capital-allocation.title: Capital Allocation
str.capital-allocation.plain_meaning:
Deciding where every marginal dollar goes — reinvest in the core, fund
new bets, acquire, pay down debt, return to owners — the CEO's actual
job once the machine runs.

str.competitive-advantage.title: Competitive Advantage
str.competitive-advantage.plain_meaning:
The durable reasons customers pick you that rivals can't quickly copy —
the moat. Real ones are structural: network effects, switching costs,
scale economies, brand memory, proprietary data or process, regulatory
position.

str.competitive-strategy.title: Competitive Strategy
str.competitive-strategy.plain_meaning:
Choosing where to compete and how to win against named rivals: Porter's
generic paths (cost leadership, differentiation, focus) and the
discipline of not being stuck between them.

str.corporate-strategy.title: Corporate Strategy
str.corporate-strategy.plain_meaning:
Managing a portfolio of businesses as one company: what to own, what to
exit, how units share strengths — and the standing question every parent
must answer: does this business become MORE valuable under our roof, or
less?

str.disruption-theory.title: Disruption Theory
str.disruption-theory.plain_meaning:
Christensen's specific mechanism (not a synonym for "new thing"): why
well-run incumbents lose to entrants whose products start WORSE —
cheaper, simpler, serving overlooked segments — then improve faster
than customer needs grow, until "worse" is suddenly good enough for
everyone.

str.five-forces.title: Five Forces
str.five-forces.plain_meaning:
Porter's model of what determines industry profitability: rivalry among
existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes,
supplier power, and buyer power — five pressures, each squeezing margin
from a different direction.

str.growth-strategy.title: Growth Strategy
str.growth-strategy.plain_meaning:
The chosen path to bigger: sell more of the same to the same (penetration),
same product to new markets, new products to the same customers, or new
to new (Ansoff's grid) — organically built or inorganically bought.

str.industry-analysis.title: Industry Analysis
str.industry-analysis.plain_meaning:
Reading an industry's structure — who captures the profit, what forces
squeeze it, where it's consolidating or fragmenting, and which way the
economics are drifting — before betting your company on a position in it.

str.innovation-strategy.title: Innovation Strategy
str.innovation-strategy.plain_meaning:
Deciding where new value will come from and protecting the work of
finding it: sustaining improvements to today's business, adjacent
extensions, and transformational bets — a portfolio with different
clocks, metrics, and management.

str.mergers-acquisitions.title: Mergers & Acquisitions
str.mergers-acquisitions.plain_meaning:
Buying growth, capability, or competition removal — valuation,
diligence, deal structure, and the part where most of the value
actually lives or dies: integration.

str.partnerships-alliances.title: Partnerships & Alliances
str.partnerships-alliances.plain_meaning:
Growth through others: channel partners who resell, technology partners
who integrate, strategic alliances that share markets or capabilities —
leverage without acquisition.

str.strategic-planning.title: Strategic Planning
str.strategic-planning.plain_meaning:
Turning direction into a coherent set of choices: Rumelt's kernel — an
honest DIAGNOSIS of the situation, a GUIDING POLICY for dealing with it,
and COHERENT ACTIONS that reinforce each other — not a wish list with
dates.

str.strategy-execution.title: Strategy Execution
str.strategy-execution.plain_meaning:
The bridge from chosen strategy to sequenced action: translating the
kernel into a few wildly important goals, cascading them into
team-level commitments, and running the cadence that keeps daily work
pointed at them.

str.swot.title: SWOT
str.swot.plain_meaning:
The structured stocktake — strengths, weaknesses, opportunities,
threats — internal capabilities crossed with external conditions.
An input to strategy, never the strategy itself.

str.vision-mission.title: Vision & Mission
str.vision-mission.plain_meaning:
What the company is FOR (mission), where it's going over a decade
(vision), and — the part that gives both teeth — what it therefore
refuses to do.

tec.ai-agents-automation.title: AI Agents & Automation
tec.ai-agents-automation.plain_meaning:
Delegating work to software that decides — multi-step tasks where the
system chooses actions, calls tools, and iterates — beyond automation
that merely repeats what it was told.

tec.ai-llms.title: AI & LLMs
tec.ai-llms.plain_meaning:
Large language models as business capabilities: machines that read,
write, summarize, extract, classify, and reason over language —
probabilistically, which is both the superpower and the fine print.

tec.apis-integration.title: APIs & Integration
tec.apis-integration.plain_meaning:
How systems talk: the contracts (what data, what format, what
promises), the sync patterns (real-time vs batch), and the failure
modes nobody designs for until they fire.

tec.bpm-workflow.title: BPM & Workflow
tec.bpm-workflow.plain_meaning:
Automating processes so work routes itself — approvals flow, handoffs
trigger, status is visible — instead of living in email threads and
somebody-remembers.

tec.build-buy-partner.title: Build, Buy or Partner
tec.build-buy-partner.plain_meaning:
The recurring capability decision: build it (control, cost, and
maintenance forever), buy it (speed and roadmap-dependency), or
partner for it (leverage and shared fate) — decided per capability,
revisited as stakes change.

tec.business-analysis.title: Business Analysis
tec.business-analysis.plain_meaning:
Turning business needs into something systems can implement: eliciting
what people actually need (vs what they ask for), modeling the process,
and bridging the two languages — business and technical — that
routinely mistranslate each other.

tec.cloud-infrastructure.title: Cloud Infrastructure
tec.cloud-infrastructure.plain_meaning:
Renting compute, storage, and services instead of owning them —
elasticity and speed in exchange for a meter that never stops running
and a landlord with opinions.

tec.crm-systems.title: CRM Systems
tec.crm-systems.plain_meaning:
The system of record for customers and revenue motion — contacts,
deals, activity, history — where the pipeline either reflects reality
or decorates it.

tec.cybersecurity-basics.title: Cybersecurity Basics
tec.cybersecurity-basics.plain_meaning:
The minimum defenses every business owes itself: MFA everywhere,
patched systems, tested backups, least-privilege access, phishing-aware
people, and a plan for the bad day — the unglamorous 20% that stops
80% of attacks.

tec.devops-release.title: DevOps & Release
tec.devops-release.plain_meaning:
Shipping changes fast without breaking production: automated pipelines,
small frequent deploys, monitoring that notices before customers do,
and rollback as a reflex rather than a crisis.

tec.digital-transformation.title: Digital Transformation
tec.digital-transformation.plain_meaning:
Changing how the business RUNS — decisions, processes, customer
experience — with technology as the lever, not the point. New tools
running old processes is renovation theater, not transformation.

tec.enterprise-architecture.title: Enterprise Architecture
tec.enterprise-architecture.plain_meaning:
The map of systems, data flows, and processes — what talks to what,
where each fact lives, which systems are load-bearing — and its fit to
what the business is trying to become.

tec.erp-systems.title: ERP Systems
tec.erp-systems.plain_meaning:
The system of record for the operating business — finance, inventory,
orders, procurement in one integrated database — where a transaction
entered once flows everywhere it's needed.

tec.master-data-management.title: Master Data Management
tec.master-data-management.plain_meaning:
One truth for the facts everything else depends on — customer, product,
vendor, price — with owned definitions, golden records, and rules for
who may change what.

tec.process-mapping.title: Process Mapping
tec.process-mapping.plain_meaning:
Drawing how work actually flows — swimlanes, decisions, handoffs
(BPMN when formality pays) — as it IS, before anyone argues about how
it should be.

tec.requirements-engineering.title: Requirements Engineering
tec.requirements-engineering.plain_meaning:
Specifying and verifying what gets built: BRDs (what the business
needs), FRDs (what the system will do), acceptance criteria (how we'll
know), and UAT (proving it with real users before go-live).

tec.technical-debt.title: Technical Debt
tec.technical-debt.plain_meaning:
Speed borrowed from the future: shortcuts, outdated foundations, and
untested tangles that made yesterday faster and make every tomorrow
slower — with interest charged in engineering hours.

evidence: cash flow statement, operating section vs P&L gross profit

evidence: dashboard usage after known data incidents

evidence: team metrics traceable to the north star

conditions: pairs actually reviewed together, not reported separately

evidence: metric improving while downstream outcome stalls

evidence: forecast error tracked and fed back

conditions: an intervention playbook exists per score band
evidence: save rate of scored-and-worked accounts vs unworked

conditions: spreadsheets operate (not just analyze) recurring processes

evidence: error findings from any audit sample

evidence: segment-level revenue/churn/CAC breakout existing at all
ICP document referencing actual segment data

evidence: value prop written per segment vs one-size
win-rate difference between ICP and non-ICP deals

unsettled positioning makes messaging unfixable — words cannot converge on a frame that does not exist
evidence: five-second test results on the homepage

concept_edges.delay: visible per deal, structural over quarters
evidence: price objections framed as competitor comparisons

evidence: discount authority rules existing or not
variance of realized prices across similar deals

the motion selects the channels — PLG feeds on content/product loops, field sales on outbound/events; mismatched channels fill the wrong funnel
evidence: conversion of each channel's leads through THIS motion

evidence: landing conversion rate vs traffic quality

evidence: CAC trend at constant spend mix

conditions: finite ICP audience in the auction channel

conditions: 6-12 months of consistent publication before the curve bends
content targets purchase-intent questions, not trivia

research design bounds segmentation truth — behavioral evidence finds segments that buy differently; opinion surveys find segments that answer differently

sample honesty vs actual buyer population

conditions: feedback is themed and weighted, not relayed raw
evidence: roadmap items sourced from patterns vs single accounts

evidence: anticipate-vs-copy ratio in recent strategy moves

evidence: positioning changes traceable to win-loss patterns

evidence: bottom-up model connecting to the GTM plan
investor pushback on sizing in past processes

motifs.name: Forecast Optimism Compounds
motifs.shape:
A financial forecast is a belief, not a fact — but incremental budgeting
converts belief into commitment automatically. An optimistic revenue
number authorizes real hiring and real purchasing before a single dollar
of it has landed. That commitment then does damage on two fronts at
once, in parallel, from the same original optimism: operating expenses
ratchet upward (because the budget base was never re-justified against
reality) which compresses margin, AND cash gets committed against revenue
that hasn't confirmed, which shortens the runway directly. Neither shows
up immediately — both surface months later, exactly when the forecast
turns out to have been wrong.

motifs.name: The Goodhart Spiral
Growth Hides Rot
motifs.shape:
The top line grows, so everyone celebrates — while margin, cash, and
quality quietly decay underneath. The growth is not separate from the
decay; the growth is *causing* the decay, and simultaneously hiding it.
Usually the first mover is an incentive — someone changed what gets
rewarded, the salesforce responded rationally, and every downstream system
faithfully amplified the distortion.

motifs.name: Incentive Eats Quality
motifs.shape:
Someone changes what gets rewarded — a bonus, a quota, a promotion
criterion, or just what leadership starts tolerating. People respond
rationally within weeks. The rewarded metric improves on schedule, the
unrewarded dimension (quality, honesty, long-term value) decays quietly,
and by the time the decay reaches customers, nobody connects it to the
incentive memo from two quarters ago.

motifs.name: One Signature, Five Consequences
motifs.shape:
The exit you're quietly aiming for — or never consciously chose — decides
what kind of money you're even allowed to take, whether you know it yet
or not. That fundraising strategy sets the mechanics of the actual deal:
the term sheet. The term sheet constructs the board, because control
provisions and board seats are negotiated at signing, not discovered
later. That board then decides whether capital gets allocated by
discipline (an investor's cold arithmetic) or by politics (whoever's
loudest in the room). And capital allocation quality is what determines,
years later, whether strategy is resourced enough to actually execute —
Sull's finding that teams execute the budget, not the speech. One
signature, at the start, quietly wrote the ending.

motifs.name: The Technical Debt Spiral
motifs.shape:
Weak customer discovery leaves product strategy with no real referee, so
the roadmap gets decided by escalation instead of evidence. An
escalation-driven roadmap crams in more than capacity allows, so every
release runs on fixed scope and a fixed deadline. Something has to give —
it's quality, invisibly. That debt then does the thing debt always does:
it charges interest. Velocity falls. And a team with less velocity has
even less room to say no to the next unreasonable deadline — so it
happens again, faster. Unlike a simple chain, this one closes into a
loop: `product-development-process → technical-debt → product-
development-process`. Once the loop starts, it feeds itself without any
new mistake being required.

motifs.name: Underpay Eats Execution
motifs.shape:
"Why isn't our strategy executing?" almost always gets investigated as a
planning problem — wrong priorities, unclear cascade, missing resources.
This motif says: check three hops further back. Below-market comp bands
quietly lower who you can hire, because the candidates with other options
take the other offer. A hiring bar eroded this way dilutes culture over
several quarters — not through one bad hire, but through the accumulated
gravity of many slightly-worse ones. And culture is precisely what
decides whether strategy survives contact with an inconvenient moment:
it's the daily behavior under pressure, not the deck. Nobody in a
strategy review checks the comp bands. That's exactly why this root
cause hides so well.
